tip: 'Nous faisons' is pronounced 'fuh-zon', not 'fay-zon' – only in forms of 'faire' does that 'ai' turn into a weak 'uh' sound.
'Viens de Lyon' means come FROM Lyon – an origin. But 'venir de' + a verb means 'just did': 'je viens de manger' = I just ate. The next word decides.
For food and drink, 'prendre' (to take) means 'to have': 'tu prends un croissant' = you're having a croissant, not grabbing one to go.
'Mettre' means 'to put', so 'tu mets la table' is literally 'you put the table' – French's way of saying 'you set the table'.
English 'leave' splits in French: 'sortir' is going out for the evening ('sors ce soir'); 'quitter' is leaving a place or person behind.
Body features usually take 'les' (the), not 'some': 'a les yeux bleus' is literally 'has THE blue eyes', not 'des yeux bleus'.
'Du café' means 'some coffee' – 'du' ('de' + 'le') is the 'some' French won't drop even where English omits it: 'qui veut du café ?'
French doesn't say your back hurts – you 'have pain at' it: 'tu as mal au dos'. Pattern: 'avoir mal à' + body part.
'Où se trouve...?' = Where is...located? More formal than 'où est...?' Both are correct.
When an adjective comes before a plural noun, 'des' usually shrinks to 'de': not 'des beaux rêves' but 'de beaux rêves'. 'Faites de beaux rêves!'
'Est-ce que' is the easiest way to form questions – just add it before a statement. No word order change needed.
Age is something you HAVE in French: 'j'ai vingt-cinq ans' is literally 'I have twenty-five years'. 'Être' here would be wrong.
'À le' is never said in French – it must contract to 'au': 'vais au cinéma', not 'à le cinéma'.
'À l'aéroport' uses the contracted 'à l'' before vowels. Full form would be 'à le', but that doesn't exist.
'Belle' comes before its noun: 'une belle maison', not 'maison belle'. A few short common adjectives ('beau', 'grand', 'petit') lead like this.
'Je suis' is both 'I am' ('être') and 'I follow' ('suivre'). Here it's following: 'je suis la leçon' = I follow the lesson, not I am it.
'Chez' means 'to/at the place of'. Use with people: 'chez le dentiste', 'chez moi' (at my place), 'chez Paul'.
The 'il' doesn't mean 'he' – it's an empty 'it': 'il me suffit d'une heure' = literally 'it suffices me an hour'. The amount you need takes 'de'.
French stays in the present with 'depuis': 'nous sommes amis depuis longtemps' is literally 'we are friends since long' for 'we have been friends'.
'Beaucoup' (much/many) normally takes plain 'de', not 'des': 'beaucoup de patience'.
Sensations are things you HAVE in French: 'ont soif' = have thirst, not 'are thirsty'. Cold and fear too: 'avoir froid', 'avoir peur'.
'Nous avons faim' is literally 'we have hunger'. Hunger is something you HAVE, not are – 'je suis faim' is wrong.
Flipping verb and subject makes a formal question: 'avez-vous un menu' = do you have a menu. Casual speech just says 'vous avez un menu ?'
'Du' is 'de' + 'le' fused: 'sort du bureau' = leaves the office, literally 'out OF the office'. 'De le' is never said.
'Avoir tort' = to be wrong, 'avoir raison' = to be right. French 'has wrong/reason'.
You HAVE dizziness in French, you don't feel it: 'j'ai le vertige' = 'I have the vertigo'. Note the 'le' – French uses 'the' where English uses none.
Nationalities aren't capitalized in French when used as adjectives: 'vous êtes français', not 'Français'.
'Être d'accord' = to agree. Literally 'to be of agreement'. Very common expression.
French is 'in anger', not 'angry': 'il est en colère'. Lots of states take 'en' this way, like 'être en retard' (late).
'Avoir confiance en' = to trust / to have confidence in. Another 'avoir' expression for a feeling.
